title: Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (2026)
description: A construction company appeals the assessment of the evasion penalty assessed after an audit discovered the business collected but did not remit sales tax over several years. It contends its actions were unintentional. The Department previously denied Taxpayer’s petition. On reconsideration, Taxpayer provides additional records as to intent and contends the Department made twenty-three legal errors regarding the evidentiary standard. The new records are insufficient to alter the determination. We do not find the evidentiary standard was improperly applied previously. Taxpayer’s petition is denied on reconsideration.

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 48
Cite as Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (2026)
BEFORE THE ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW AND HEARINGS DIVISION
DEPARTMENT OF REVENUE
STATE OF WASHINGTON
In the Matter of the Petition for Correction of ) D E T E R M I N A T I O N
Assessment of )
) No. 23-0075R
. . . )
) Registration No. . . .
)
RCW 82.32.090; RCW 82.02.010; WAC 458-20-228 – EVIDENCE OF INTENT
TO EVADE – The Department has the burden of proving a taxpayer’s evasion by
clear, cogent, and convincing evidence. The Department looks to the actions of the
corporate entity as a whole when determining evasion. Failing to remit retail sales
tax creates a prima facie case against the Taxpayer. The taxpayer may then rebut
the Department’s prima facie case.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
for in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
Kelly, T.R.O. – A construction company appeals the assessment of the evasion penalty assessed
after an audit discovered the business collected but did not remit sales tax over several years. It
contends its actions were unintentional. The Department previously denied Taxpayer’s petition.
On reconsideration, Taxpayer provides additional records as to intent and contends the Department
made twenty-three legal errors regarding the evidentiary standard. The new records are insufficient
to alter the determination. We do not find the evidentiary standard was improperly applied
previously. Taxpayer’s petition is denied on reconsideration.1
ISSUES
1. Did the Department properly uphold the evasion penalty under RCW 82.32.090(7) and WAC
458-20-228 (Rule 228)?
2. Does the additional documentation provided by Taxpayer rebut the Department’s prima facie
[case] showing the evasion penalty should apply under Rule 228?
FINDINGS OF FACT
We incorporate the facts set forth in Determination No. 23-0075 by reference and restate only
those relevant to our discussion here.
1
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 49
. . . (Taxpayer) is a construction business focusing on plaster installation [and] based in . . .
Washington. The Department of Revenue’s Audit Division (Audit) audited Taxpayer for the period
of January 1, 2018, through December 31, 2021 (Audit Period).
Taxpayer is a family run business. . . . (Owner) owns the business. Owner hired his daughter . . .
(Daughter) as the bookkeeper in early 2018. Daughter had no prior bookkeeping or accounting
background, having just graduated college with a degree in biology. Pursuant to Taxpayer’s
petition, Daughter’s training consisted of Taxpayer’s prior accountant giving her some instruction
during which, “[Owner] assumed the accountant would address all Washington excise tax
reporting,” and “[Daughter] did not receive the training on excise taxes [Owner] assumed she had.”
According to Taxpayer’s petition, Taxpayer previously, “had some difficulty with reporting,”
where Taxpayer overpaid tax for more than four years. With the help of an outside accountant,
Taxpayer got a refund for four years of overpayment.
Taxpayer’s petition claims that Owner retained control of billing even after Daughter took over
the accounting. He billed customers in Excel with invoices that listed retail sales tax as a distinct
charge. Daughter’s accounting consisted of using Quickbooks, bank statements, customer checks,
and the Department’s website to file taxes, track job costs and profitability, and generally maintain
the books. She used Quickbooks to record expenses and input deposits, but never used it or any
other program for invoicing. Neither Quickbooks nor the bank statements showed sales tax
separately itemized, and Daughter asserts that she did not look at the invoices from Excel showing
sales tax until late 2019. Daughter contends she was unaware that Taxpayer was collecting retail
sales tax from customers. Daughter said, “In summary, there was a separation where my dad would
invoice, and I would submit the taxes.” Taxpayer’s Petition, Exhibit 1, page 1.
During the Audit Period, Taxpayer reported income mainly under the wholesaling B&O tax
classification. Taxpayer only reported under the retailing and retail sales tax classifications once
in November 2021. During the Audit Period, Taxpayer remitted $. . . in retail sales tax. Audit
found sales invoices showing Taxpayer had collected retail sales tax but had not remitted it to the
Department. Taxpayer collected and failed to remit a total of $. . . in retail sales tax during the
Audit Period.
Audit issued a Notice of Balance Due letter . . . on June 14, 2022, for a total of $. . . , comprising
$. . . in tax adjustments, $. . . in penalties, and $. . . in interest to that point.
Audit gave credit on overreported wholesaling B&O tax and asserted retailing B&O and retail
sales tax on sales where retail sales tax was collected but not remitted. Audit also asserted retail
sales tax on wholesale sales due to missing reseller permits. Audit applied a fifty percent evasion
penalty on the retail sales tax Taxpayer collected but did not remit.
Taxpayer timely petitioned for review of the fifty percent evasion penalty. Taxpayer attempts to
rebut the Department’s finding of evasion, contending that the failure to remit retail sales tax was
unintentional. Taxpayer’s petition was denied in Det. No 23-0075. We held that the evasion
penalty was appropriate as Taxpayer knew a tax liability was due, and Taxpayer attempted to avoid
taxation through intentional wrongdoing. We further held that after Taxpayer’s attempt to rebut

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 50
this evidence, the evidence of evasion weighed heavily in favor of upholding the evasion
assessment.
Taxpayer timely filed for reconsideration. On reconsideration, Taxpayer submitted additional
records and argument. Taxpayer provided a number of new records. We summarize them as
additional records demonstrating Daughter’s inexperience in her position, Taxpayer’s transition to
working as a prime contractor in 2018, various bank deposit records, and records of specific
discounts given. Audit reviewed these records thoroughly.
Taxpayer’s additional arguments consist of identifying what Taxpayer terms twenty-three separate
errors in the Department’s determination. In doing so, Taxpayer reinterprets what it believes
should be necessary to prove evasion and terms the application of the current legal standard as
errors. Taxpayer interprets the intent element as applying to individual actors rather than the
Taxpayer itself.
ANALYSIS
The legal requirements for evasion remain the same as in our initial determination. Here we
reanalyze the facts, including the additional information provided on reconsideration, based on the
same law. As such, we reiterate our prior explanation of the laws and rules.
The Department is required to assess a fifty percent penalty if it finds that any deficiency resulted
from an intent to evade a tax. RCW 82.32.090(7). This is further explained by Rule 228,
specifically:
The evasion penalty is imposed when a taxpayer knows a tax liability is due but
attempts to escape detection or payment of the tax liability through deceit, fraud, or
other intentional wrongdoing. An intent to evade does not exist where a deficiency
is the result of an honest mistake, miscommunication, or the lack of knowledge
regarding proper accounting methods. The department has the burden of showing
the existence of an intent to evade a tax liability through clear, cogent and
convincing evidence.
Rule 228(5)(f). We summarize Rule 228 as having two elements. First, that a taxpayer knew a tax
liability was due. Second, that same taxpayer attempts to avoid taxation through intentional
wrongdoing.
The Department has the burden of proving both elements of evasion by clear, cogent, and
convincing evidence. Id. Clear, cogent, and convincing evidence has been described as evidence
convincing the trier of fact that the fact at issue is “highly probable,” or stated another way, the
evidence relied upon must be “clear, positive and unequivocal in [its] implication.” Colonial
Imports, Inc. v. Carlton Northwest, Inc., 121 Wn.2d 726, 735, 853 P.2d 913 (1993).
To meet this burden, the Department must present objective and credible evidence that clearly
demonstrates intent to evade a known tax liability; mere suspicion of intent to evade is not enough
to meet this burden. Det. No. 03-0147, 22 WTD 274, 276 (2003). “Intent is a state of mind. As

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 51
such, it must usually be proved by circumstantial evidence.” State v. LaRue, 5 Wn. App. 299, 306,
487 P.2d 255 (1971). Circumstantial evidence carries the same weight as direct evidence, and
constitutes evidence that allows for reasonable inferences based on common sense and experience.
See State v. Hieb, 107 Wn.2d 97, 111, 727 P.2d 239 (1986). Mere underreporting of collected
retail sales tax does not constitute evasion. Det. No. 98-065, 17 WTD 359, 371 (1998) (evasion
not found where the taxpayer claimed underreporting was due to dishonest bartenders). However,
substantial underreporting of collected retail sales tax does constitute evasion. Det. No. 97-134R,
18 WTD 163, 167 (1999) (evasion found where the taxpayer filed “no business” returns when it
had gross receipts and also failed to remit collected retail sales tax).
Rule 228 lays out a nonexclusive list of taxpayer actions for consideration of intent to evade. The
one example relevant to this analysis is, “The willful failure of a seller to remit retail sales taxes
collected from customers to the department.” Rule 228(5)(f)(ii)(B).
We have previously held that failing to remit retail sales tax creates a prima facie case against the
Taxpayer, stating:
The Board of Tax Appeals has said that in the case of the retail sales tax, a prima
facie showing of fiduciary fraud, and hence a prima facie showing of tax evasion,
is made simply by showing that the seller has collected and failed to turn over the
funds to [the Department]. A seller, as trustee of retail sales tax funds collected
from purchasers, stands in a fiduciary relationship with the state. A trustee owes to
the beneficiary of the trust the highest degree of good faith, diligence, loyalty, and
integrity; a trustee must act solely in the beneficiary's interest. Unexcused failure
to timely turn over trust funds actually collected by a seller on behalf of the state is
a breach of the seller's fiduciary duty, and amounts as a matter of law to fraud on
the state. .
Det. No. 04-0098, 23 WTD 331 (2004) (citing Sunrise Fiberglass Engineering v. Dept. of Revenue,
BTA Docket No. 41913, 13 WTD 203 (1993), and David Grimes v. Dept. of Revenue, BTA Docket
No. 51276 (1998)).
In the same determination we went on to state that the taxpayer may then rebut the Department’s
prima facie case, stating:
Once [the Department] has clearly demonstrated the existence of each of the
elements of evasion, a burden of production is imposed on the taxpayer to come
forward with evidence of honest mistake, ignorance of the law, negligence, or some
other fact which tends to rebut [the Department]’s evidence. Mere subjective and
self-serving statements by the taxpayer regarding intent, without more, are
insufficient to meet this burden of production. Any evidence presented by the
taxpayer must be weighed against that presented by [the Department]. Because the
burden placed on the taxpayer is one of production only, the burden of proof as to
evasion still rests with [the Department]. The evidence of evasion presented by
[the Department] when viewed alone, or along with the taxpayer's evidence, must
weigh heavily in favor of upholding the assessment.

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 52
Id. We also held that business experience tends to undercut or negate the possibility that a taxpayer
was unaware that it was required to report and pay taxes. Id.
1. Did the Department make errors in applying the legal standard to uphold an evasion penalty
under Rule 228?
In the petition for reconsideration, Taxpayer asserts arguments advancing an alternative
evidentiary standard wherein the intent of the individuals working for Taxpayer should be
separately analyzed.
The statute on penalties, including the evasion penalty, applies to “taxpayers.” See RCW
82.32.090. This is further explained by Rule 228, specifically:
The evasion penalty is imposed when a taxpayer knows a tax liability is due but
attempts to escape detection or payment of the tax liability through deceit, fraud, or
other intentional wrongdoing.
Rule 228(5)(f) (emphasis added).
Chapter 82.32 does not define a number of terms including “taxpayer” directly but rather cross
references chapters 82.01 through 82.27 for applicable definitions. In Chapter 82.02 we find a
definition for “taxpayer” which states:
“Taxpayer” includes any individual, group of individuals, corporation, or
association liable for any tax or the collection of any tax hereunder, or who engages
in any business or performs any act for which a tax is imposed by this title.
"Taxpayer" also includes any person liable for any fee or other charge collected by
the department under any provision of law, including registration assessments and
delinquency fees imposed.
RCW 82.02.010. We read this to mean that the liability for the tax is what creates a “taxpayer.”
Neither Owner nor Daughter are primarily personally liable for the tax due by Taxpayer. Taxpayer
is liable for its own taxes. In this circumstance, references to the term “taxpayer” are read to apply
to the corporate entity as it has the primary liability. Thus, when evaluating whether the criteria
for evasion are met, we look at the actions of the tax-paying entity as a whole.
Upon review, we find the Department’s application of the evidentiary standard with the corporate
entity Taxpayer as the “taxpayer” in this circumstance to be consistent with prior interpretation of
rules and statutes. We are not persuaded that there is any legal basis upon which we should grant
the relief requested. We deny the petition as to this issue.
2. Does the additional documentation provided by Taxpayer alter the outcome of the application
of the evasion penalty under Rule 228?

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 53
Taxpayer provided a number of new records. We summarize them as additional records
demonstrating Daughter’s inexperience in her position, Taxpayer’s transition to working as a
prime contractor in 2018, various bank deposit records, and records of specific discounts given.
Neither the assorted bank records nor the records of specific discounts given reveal any new
information. Thus, they do not have any impact on the legal analysis of the application of the
evasion penalty.
Both Daughter’s inexperience and Taxpayer’s transition to working as a prime contractor represent
evidence put forth by Taxpayer on reconsideration to rebut the Department’s prima facie showing
of evasion.
Once the Department has clearly established the elements of evasion, a burden of production is
imposed on the taxpayer to produce evidence of honest mistake, miscommunication, ignorance of
law, lack of knowledge, or some other fact that tends to rebut the Department’s evidence. Det. No.
16-0066, 35 WTD 540 (2016). However, mere subjective and self-serving statements by the
taxpayer regarding intent, without more, are insufficient to meet this burden of production. 23
WTD at 338.
Daughter’s inexperience in her position was unquestioned and previously considered. Cumulative
evidence on this topic is unpersuasive.
Taxpayer’s transition to a prime contractor represents lack of experience in collecting retail sales
tax. While Taxpayer previously advanced this argument in its initial petition, it was not explicitly
considered in the prior determination as irrelevant. We reiterate, in this case Taxpayer charged and
then failed to remit sales tax. This is not a circumstance where Taxpayer under collected, remitted
late, or didn’t know it needed to collect tax in the first place. Taxpayer charging, collecting, and
failing to remit over $. . . of retail sales tax over a period of years wholly obviates any suggestion
that inexperience played a role.
We do not find Taxpayer’s new records have any impact on our prior analysis. We sustain the
assessment of the evasion penalty.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer's petition is denied on reconsideration.
Dated this 1st day of September 2023.
